title: How do I get there?
goal: Ask strangers for directions and — harder — understand the answer. Along the way, master the imperative, which Russian uses far more often than English does.
bekal: ask for directions with standard phrases
understand directions: right, left, straight, turn
ask people to repeat or slow down

dialogs.title: Диалог — Looking for the post office
dialogs.intro: Ani needs to send a package to Indonesia and doesn't know where the post office is. Notice the imperative forms used by the person answering — they all end in -ите.

lines.speaker: Ани:
lines.id: Excuse me, could you tell me where the post office is around here?
lines.literal: excuse-me, tell, please, where — here — post-office?

lines.speaker: Прохожий:
lines.id: The post office? Go straight to the traffic light.

lines.speaker: Прохожий:
lines.id: Then turn left. There'll be a pharmacy there.
lines.literal: then — turn — to-the-left. there — will-be — pharmacy.

lines.speaker: Прохожий:
lines.id: The post office is across from the pharmacy. A big blue building.
lines.literal: post-office — opposite — pharmacy. big — blue — building.

lines.speaker: Прохожий:
lines.id: No, about five minutes on foot.

lines.speaker: Ани:
lines.id: Sorry, could you repeat that? Straight, then…?

lines.speaker: Прохожий:
lines.id: Straight to the traffic light, left, and the post office is on the right.
lines.literal: straight — until — traffic-light, to-the-left, and — post-office — on-the-right.

lines.speaker: Прохожий:
lines.id: You're welcome. If you get lost, just ask again.
lines.literal: not — for — what. if — get-lost, ask — again — time.

notes: **Imperatives in Russian are polite, not rude.** ⚠️ *Идите прямо* (go straight), *Скажите* (tell me), *Повторите* (repeat) — all imperatives, and all perfectly polite once you add **пожалуйста**. English speakers tend to soften requests with "could you…?"; in Russian, avoiding the imperative is what sounds odd and roundabout.
**There are two imperative forms: -и/-й for ты, -ите/-йте for вы.** *Скажи* (to a friend) vs. *Скажите* (to a stranger). *Иди* vs. *Идите*. The choice follows the same ты/вы rule as in Unit 1.

**Налево / направо mean "to the left / to the right"; слева / справа mean "on the left / on the right."** ⚠️ The same moving-vs.-staying difference as куда vs. где in Unit 13. *Поверните налево* (turn left) but *Почта справа* (the post office is on the right).
**Минут пять means "about five minutes."** Flipping the number and the noun turns it into an estimate — the trick you met in Unit 12. Very common in directions, since nobody measures exactly.

**Как пройти is for walking, как доехать for transport.** It pairs with идти/ехать from Unit 13. *Как пройти до почты?* (how do I walk to the post office?), *Как доехать до вокзала?* (how do I get to the station?). After до, always the genitive.
**Спасибо большое is warmer than plain спасибо.** Other forms: *Огромное спасибо* (thanks a million), *Спасибо вам большое*. For help that really matters, Russians use the long form.

**Don't expect short directions.** Russians tend to give full directions with landmarks, and they rarely simplify them for foreigners. Two lifesaving phrases: *Повторите, пожалуйста* and *Помедленнее, пожалуйста* (a bit slower, please).

grammars.title: The imperative
body: Take the **они** form of the verb, drop the ending, then add **-и / -ите** (if what's left ends in a consonant) or **-й / -йте** (if it ends in a vowel).
after: Now you know why **извините**, **скажите**, **повторите**, **подождите**, and **смотрите** all end the same way: they're all imperatives addressed to вы. Words you've used since Unit 1 turn out to be one family.
⚠️ To forbid, use **не** + imperative: *Не беспокойтесь* (don't worry), *Не спешите* (don't rush). To suggest doing something together, use **давайте**: *Давайте пойдём* (let's go).

grammars.title: Direction words
body: Watch the moving / staying pairs — this is where most mistakes happen.
after: *Поверните **направо*** — turn right. *Магазин **справа*** — the store is on the right.
Other common landmark words: **напротив** (opposite), **рядом с** (next to), **между** (between), **за углом** (around the corner), **через дорогу** (across the street).

Say it
English
rows: Could you tell me where … is?
How do I get to …? (by transport)

blocks.title: Покажите на карте — the real lifesaver
items: Spoken directions in Russian are long and fast, and beginners almost always lose track by the second sentence. **Покажите на карте, пожалуйста** moves the whole conversation onto a picture, and nearly every Russian is happy to do it.
Its partner: **Напишите, пожалуйста** (please write it down). Street and station names are much easier to read than to hear.
⚠️ Don't pretend to understand. Nodding and then walking off in the wrong direction is the most common way tourists get lost in Moscow. Asking twice is completely normal, and nobody is offended.

exercises.prompt: Change to the imperative addressed to вы.
Put the words in the right order.

items: Could you tell me where the post office is?
Go straight to the traffic light.
The pharmacy is on the right.
Please show me on the map.
